prompt: A calculated field `Price per bag` has the formula `=Revenue/Bags`. What does its grand total cell compute?
hint: The field never sees a row, in any cell.

choices.text: The average of the six product rows above it
choices.why: Averaging the rows would weigh a product with 24 bags the same as one with 200. The field divides the totals instead.

choices.text: Total revenue ÷ total bags: 51,494 ÷ 591
choices.why: Right. Every cell, the grand total included, applies the formula to the sums in that cell: R$ 87.13 a bag.

choices.text: The sum of the six product values above it
choices.why: That is what Sum of would mean for an ordinary field. A calculated field's grand total applies the formula again, to the grand totals.

choices.text: The average of the 108 prices in the Price column
choices.why: That is Average of Price, R$ 75.07, where every sale counts once whatever its size.

prompt: A calculated field `Revenue 2` has the formula `=Price*Bags`. What does it show for `CER250`?
hint: Multiply the sum of the prices of its 11 sales by the sum of their bags.

prompt: For `SUL1K`, `Average of Price` is 121.00 and the calculated field `Price per bag` is 118.44. Why do they differ?
hint: Sale S1002 sold 17 bags at R$ 116.

choices.text: The calculated field rounds each sale's price to whole reais before it divides
choices.why: Nothing is rounded; 118.44 is 118.4382 shown with two decimals.

choices.text: Each sale counts once in one, each bag once in the other
choices.why: Right. Wholesale orders are large and pay less than list, so they weigh more in the price per bag than in the average of prices.

choices.text: Average of Price leaves out the wholesale sales, which pay less than list
choices.why: It includes all 21 sales of SUL1K; each simply counts once.

choices.text: One of the two is wrong, and a SUMIFS shows which
choices.why: Both are right answers to different questions, and the SUMIFS formulas of the section agree with each.

prompt: To pay a bonus of 5% on sales of more than ten bags, somebody adds a calculated field `=IF(Bags>10, Revenue*0.05, 0)`. What does its grand total show?
hint: Ask what Bags means inside a calculated field's grand total cell.

choices.text: 5% of all revenue, since the cell's total bags, 591, exceed ten
choices.why: Right. IF tests the sum in the cell, not each sale, so every sale's revenue is in the bonus, large or small.

choices.text: 5% of the revenue of only those sales that were over ten bags
choices.why: That needs the test made on each row, which a calculated field never does. A column in the table can do it.

choices.text: Zero, because a calculated field cannot use IF
choices.why: It can use IF. The trouble is what IF is given: totals, not rows.

choices.text: An error, because Bags names a whole column of the table, not one cell
choices.why: Excel accepts the formula and shows a number, which is what makes the mistake easy to miss.

prompt: A formula that has to be worked out sale by sale, such as price times bags, belongs in a ___ of the table, and the pivot then sums it.
hint: Lesson 2 did this for Revenue.

prompt: Which of these give a right answer as a calculated field? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read each one aloud with total in front of every field.

choices.text: `=Revenue/Bags`, the revenue of an average bag
choices.why: Total revenue over total bags is a real quantity.

choices.text: `=Price*Bags`, to rebuild the revenue
choices.why: A total of prices measures nothing; the product has to be made on each row first.

choices.text: `=(Revenue-Cost)/Revenue`, with `Cost` a column of the table
choices.why: Total profit over total revenue is the margin of the whole cell, weighted correctly.

choices.text: `=IF(Price>100, Bags, 0)`, the bags sold above R$ 100 a bag
choices.why: IF would test the sum of the prices in the cell, which is above 100 almost everywhere.

prompt: With the calculated item `Direct` (`=Online+Shop`) in the `Channel` field, what grand total does the pivot table show for `Sum of Revenue`?
hint: The real total plus the item.

prompt: Why is the grand total wrong once `Direct` is added as a calculated item?
hint: Where is each online sale counted now?

choices.text: Excel rounds the calculated item before adding it
choices.why: Nothing is rounded; the item is exactly 12,763.

choices.text: The item makes every pivot cell an average instead of a sum
choices.why: The other cells are unchanged; only a row was added.

choices.text: Online and Shop are counted twice
choices.why: Right. The grand total adds every row of the field, the new one included, so 12,763 is counted twice.

choices.text: A calculated item only works with Count, not Sum
choices.why: It works with Sum; that is exactly how it produced 12,763.

prompt: The sales team wants `Direct` against `Wholesale` in three different reports. Where should `Direct` be made?
hint: Ask whether it is a fact about each sale.

choices.text: In a column of the table, such as `Route`, which every report reads
choices.why: Right. A fact about each row belongs in a column; every pivot table, formula and chart then reads it.

choices.text: In a calculated item, copied into each of the three reports
choices.why: Each copy carries the double-counted grand total and a formula nobody sees.

choices.text: In a group made separately in each report
choices.why: A group is right for one pivot table; three groups are three places to keep the same rule.

choices.text: In a calculated field `=Online+Shop`
choices.why: A calculated field combines fields, not items of one field; Online is not a field.

prompt: Put the steps that group `Online` and `Shop` under `Direct` in order.
hint: Select, group, then name.
items: Click Online in the pivot table
trap: Renaming comes last: there is no Group1 to rename until the group exists.

prompt: What does a slicer give that the same field in the Filters area does not?
hint: Think of somebody else opening the sheet.

choices.text: It shows on the sheet which items are selected
choices.why: Right. A Filters field with two items chosen reads (Multiple Items); a slicer lights the buttons.

choices.text: It filters by a different rule, keeping rows instead of hiding them
choices.why: Both filter the same way; the slicer only draws it.

choices.text: It is the only way to filter by a field that is not in Rows
choices.why: The Filters area does that too; the field sits there.

choices.text: It recalculates the source table
choices.why: Neither touches the table; both filter what the pivot table reads.

prompt: With the `Channel` slicer on `Wholesale`, what does the `Report` pivot table show for `SUL1K`?
hint: Or the SUMIFS of the section, with two conditions.

prompt: With `Wholesale` lit, `CER250` and `SUL250` disappear from the pivot table. What does that tell you?
hint: Look at who buys 250 g bags of those two.

choices.text: The slicer hides the two smallest products by default
choices.why: A slicer hides nothing by size; it keeps the rows of the chosen items.

choices.text: No wholesale customer ever bought either of them
choices.why: Right. Every sale of CER250 and SUL250 was online or in the shop, so there is nothing wholesale to show.

choices.text: Their rows were deleted from the table Sales
choices.why: A slicer never changes the table; clear it and both come back.

choices.text: The pivot table needs refreshing after a slicer is added
choices.why: A slicer acts at once; nothing is out of date.

prompt: A `Product` slicer sits beside the `Channel` slicer, which has `Wholesale` lit. `CER250` is drawn faded in the `Product` slicer. What does the fading mean?
hint: Two slicers on one pivot table answer each other.

choices.text: CER250 is excluded and cannot be clicked until Wholesale is cleared
choices.why: It can still be clicked; the fading only reports that nothing matches.

choices.text: CER250 has no rows left once the other slicer's choice is applied
choices.why: Right. The item exists, but no wholesale sale contains it.

choices.text: CER250 has been removed from the table Products
choices.why: The slicer reads the sales, and the product is still there.

choices.text: CER250 is selected, since faded buttons are the chosen ones
choices.why: Chosen buttons are lit; faded ones have no data under the current selection.

prompt: The data ends in June 2026. Why does the lesson compare January to June 2026 with January to June 2025, rather than with all of 2025?
hint: Count the months on each side.

choices.text: A timeline cannot select a whole year
choices.why: It can, with Years chosen; the problem is the comparison, not the control.

choices.text: Excel's timeline always shows six months at a time
choices.why: It shows years, quarters, months or days, and selects any span.

choices.text: Because 2025 has more wholesale customers
choices.why: Customers have nothing to do with it; the number of months does.

choices.text: Twelve months against six is not like with like
choices.why: Right. All of 2025 is R$ 35,551 and would make any half year look like a collapse.

prompt: With the timeline on January to June 2026 and every `Channel` button lit, what is the grand total of revenue?
hint: The SUMIFS of the section with two dates checks it.

prompt: **Insert Timeline** offers no field at all on somebody's pivot table, although their data has a Date column. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: The dialog lists fields by what their values are.

choices.text: The dates are text, not dates
choices.why: Right. A timeline needs real dates, which is what lesson 6 repairs.

choices.text: A timeline needs Date to be in Rows first
choices.why: It needs no field in the layout, like a slicer.

choices.text: Only one timeline is allowed per workbook
choices.why: A workbook can hold several; the dialog would still list the field.

choices.text: The pivot table has a slicer already
choices.why: A slicer and a timeline work together on one pivot table, as the section shows.

prompt: A pivot table built from a copy of the sales pasted onto another sheet does not appear in the slicer's **Report Connections**. Why?
hint: What does a slicer actually filter?

choices.text: Report Connections lists only pivot tables on the slicer's own sheet
choices.why: It lists pivot tables on any sheet, with the sheet named beside each.

choices.text: The copy has a cache of its own
choices.why: Right. Build the pivot table again from the table Sales and it joins the list.

choices.text: A slicer can never be connected to more than one pivot table
choices.why: The section connects one slicer to two.

choices.text: The copied pivot table needs a slicer of its own on the same field first
choices.why: A second slicer would filter it separately; it would not put it on the list.

prompt: After grouping `Date` by years in `ByYear`, somebody drags `Date` into the rows of `ByProduct` and it arrives already grouped by years. What explains it?
hint: Where does a grouping live?

choices.text: Excel copies the last grouping used to any new date field
choices.why: There is no such memory; the grouping belongs to something the two pivot tables have in common.

choices.text: ByProduct is connected to the same slicer, and slicers carry groupings
choices.why: Slicers filter; they carry no grouping.

choices.text: The two share a pivot cache, and the grouping was made in that cache
choices.why: Right. Refresh, grouping and calculated fields all belong to the cache, so every pivot table on it shares them.

choices.text: The table Sales gained a column of years when the grouping was made
choices.why: Grouping never touches the table; the table still has eight columns.

prompt: With the slicer connected to both pivot tables and `Wholesale` lit, how many bags does `ByYear` show for 2026?
hint: Wholesale sales only, January to June 2026.

prompt: F5 holds `=B5` and F6 holds `=GETPIVOTDATA("Revenue",$A$3,"Product","CER250")`, both showing 837. Then `Wholesale` is clicked in the slicer. What happens?
hint: CER250 has no wholesale sales, so its row leaves the pivot table.

choices.text: Both show 0, because CER250 sold nothing wholesale
choices.why: Neither shows 0: one reads whatever moved into B5, the other reports that CER250 is gone.

choices.text: Both keep showing 837 until somebody refreshes the pivot table
choices.why: A slicer acts at once, and both formulas follow the pivot table.

choices.text: F5 shows DEC250's 1,330 with no warning, and F6 shows #REF!
choices.why: Right. The plain reference reads the cell; GETPIVOTDATA looks for CER250 by name and says it is not there.

choices.text: F5 shows #REF! and F6 shows DEC250's 1,330
choices.why: It is the other way round: the name cannot be found, the position always can.

prompt: Match each argument of `=GETPIVOTDATA("Revenue",$A$3,"Product","CER1K")` to what it says.
hint: Which number, which pivot table, which cell.

pairs.right: Which pivot table to read it from
Which cell of that pivot table

right_distractors: Which sheet the answer is written to

prompt: With every button lit, `=GETPIVOTDATA("Revenue",$A$3,"Product","CER1K")` answers 21,356. What does it answer with `Wholesale` lit?
hint: Does it read the table or the pivot table?

choices.text: 21,356, because GETPIVOTDATA ignores slicers
choices.why: It reads the pivot table as shown, filters included. A SUMIFS on the table is the way to ignore slicers.

choices.text: 17,168, what the pivot shows under that slicer
choices.why: Right. GETPIVOTDATA returns what the pivot table shows, so it changes with every slicer and timeline.

choices.text: #REF!, because a slicer is active
choices.why: #REF! comes only when the named item is not in the pivot table; CER1K is.

choices.text: 38,731, the wholesale grand total
choices.why: That is what it gives with no field and item pairs at all.

prompt: `=GETPIVOTDATA("Revenue",$A$3)`, with no field and item pairs, returns the ___ total of the pivot table.
hint: The bottom row.

prompt: A table has `Revenue` and a `Cost` column. One analyst adds a per-row `Margin %` column and shows its Average in a pivot; another adds a calculated field `=(Revenue-Cost)/Revenue`. Which gives the margin of the whole business?
hint: A one-bag sale and a twenty-bag sale: should they count the same?

choices.text: The average of Margin %, because it looks at every sale
choices.why: It looks at every sale and weighs a one-bag sale the same as a twenty-bag one, so it is not the margin of the money.

choices.text: Both, since they always give the same number
choices.why: They agree only when every sale has the same revenue, which these do not.

choices.text: Neither: margin can only be computed with SUMIFS
choices.why: SUMIFS can check it, but the calculated field is right on its own.

choices.text: The calculated field: total profit over total revenue
choices.why: Right. A ratio of two totals is the kind of formula a calculated field gets right, and it weighs each sale by its money.

prompt: Match each tool of this lesson to the job it does well.
hint: One description fits none of them.

pairs.right: A ratio of two totals, in every cell
A filter by a field, visible on the sheet
A filter by a span of dates
One pivot value, found by its names

right_distractors: A new row that adds other rows of its field
